2. The plaintiff's case in brief is that the land in suit comprises a plot of land being C. S Plot No.310 measuring '80 acre, which was recorded, along with CS. Plot No.311 measuring .08 acre, as Koljote of one Mainuddin, the predecessor-in-interest of Defendants No.2 to 9, in Khatian No.83 of mouza Rajarbagh P.S. Tejgaon, under the Jote of one Mani Mohan Dutta, which was recorded in Khatian No.82 of the mouza under the superior interest of one Haladhar Dey Sarkar. The father's name of Mainuddin was wrongly mentioned to be Ainuddin in Khatian No.83 in place of his correct name of Amir. The jote of Mani Mohan Dutta was put to auction in execution of a decree for arrears of rent obtained by Haladhar Dey Sarker and purchased by the decree-holder on 6-7-38. The sale was confirmed on 11-8-38 and delivery of possession of the auction purchased property was taken through Court on 23-1-39. The decree-holder auction purchaser having possessed the land for sometime settled the land of C S Plot No.311, on which the homestead was situated, with Mainuddin, son of Amir, at an annual rent of Rs. 1/6/-annas on the basis of a Kabuliyat executed on 27-3-39 and registered on 1-4-39. The other plot, namely C S. Plot No.310, remained in the khas possession of the auction-purchaser till 15-1-41, when the same was settled with the predecessor of plaintiffs No.1 to 18, and plaintiff No.19 off behalf of himself and on behalf of plaintiff No.20, on the basis of a registered Kabuliyat of the said date. Taking advantage of the wrong recording of the father's name of Mainuddin in the record-of-right defendant No.10 who happened to be an Advocate of the Dacca High Court, along with his relative defendant No.11, created some Kabalas in collusion with the heirs of Mainuddin to grab a portion of the land which has become valuable in the meantime. A dispute having arisen as to the possession of the land, defendant No.3, initiated a proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, in which possession having been found by the Magistrate, who was trying proceeding, in favour of the defendants, possession has been taken by the defendants from the receiver who had been appointed by the said Magistrate in the said proceeding. 

 3. Two sets of written statement were filed in this case, one by Defendants No.1 to 9 and the other by Defendants No.10 and 11 and the contentions raised therein are more or less the same. According to the contesting defendants, Mainuddin was a holder of an occupancy raiyati-right and was recorded as such in C.S. Khatian No.83 and his father's name also was correctly recorded therein as Ainuddin. The alleged auction sale of the interest of Mani Mohan Dutta, the landlord of Mainuddin is not true and, even if there had been any such auction-sale it did not affect the interest of Mainuddin, as it was a protected interest under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. In case, however, such an interest is held to be an encumbrance it had not been annulled by service of a notice, as required under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The story of granting settlement by the alleged auction purchaser of C.S. Plot No.311 to Mainuddin or of C.S. Plot No.310 to the plaintiffs is without any foundation and Mainuddin and his heirs, during the old age of Mainuddin, and after his death, during the minority of Defendants No.2 and 3, had all along been in possession of the disputed land through the plaintiffs and their predecessors as bargadars. 

 11. At the outset it may be pointed out that the view of the learned Judges of the High Court that the defendants had no locus standi to claim any interest in the suit land in the context of their allegation as to the father's name of Mainuddin being Ainuddin was misconceived. The father's name of Mainuddin was found to be Amir and not Ainuddin as wrongly stated in the C.S. Khatian No.83. The case of the plaintiffs in this regard was accepted and that of the defendant's was rejected, by the said courts. It was the plaintiff's case that defendants No.1-9 was successors-in-interest of Mainuddin who was the holder of the land recorded in Khatian No.83. The defence case on this question was also the same. The difference between the two cases was only in respect of the father's name of Mainuddin. According to the plaintiff, it was Amir, as was mentioned in the Kabuliyat Ext.3, and not Ainuddin as was mentioned in the Khatian Ext. 6, but according to the defence, it was Ainuddin and not Amir and it has been correctly stated in the Khatian Ext.6. The learned Judges of the High Court have observed that as defendants No.1-9 had admittedly no connection with Mainuddin, son of Amir, the Courts below ought to have held that these defendants had no locus standi to claim the suit land. It is not the case of the plaintiffs nor of the defendants that there were two Mainuddin, one being the son of Ainuddin and the other being the son of Amir and that the disputed land belonged either to Mainuddin son of Ainuddin or Maiauddin son of Amir. The findings of both the Courts below on this question were also that the defendants were the successors of Mainuddin, who was admittedly the holder of the land of Khatian No.83, but the father's name of the said Mainuddin was not Ainuddin, as claimed by the defendants, but was Amir, as asserted by the plaintiffs; So the observation of the learned Judges on this question that the Courts below ought to have held that the defendants had no locus standi to claim the suit land is based upon some misapprehension. 

 12. As has been indicated above, the learned Judges of the High Court disagreed with the concurrent finding of the two Courts below rejecting the plea of the settlement advanced by the plaintiffs. The plaintiff’s case of separate settlement of each of the two plots of land, appertaining to Khatian No.83 of Mouza Rajarbagh, after their auction purchase by the heirs of Haladhar Dey Sarker, one with Mainuddin by Ext.3 and the other with the plaintiffs by Ext. 3(a) was disbelieved by the learned Subordinate Judge on the grounds that the heir of Haladhar Dey Sarkar did not acquire any right, title and interest in the disputed lands and had, therefore, no authority to settle such land, that the case of surrender of the lands of Khatian No.83 by Maiauddin to the auction purchasers, which was not pleaded but was argued at the time of trial was very improbable and that the settlement by Ext.3 with Mainuddin of only C.S. Plot No.311 measuring .08 acre on which a part of his homestead was situated, the remaining part of the homestead, having been upon the other plot, was not acceptable in the facts and circumstances of the case. In the context of these findings the question of genuineness of the rent receipts, Ext. 4 series, which were produced by the plaintiffs in support of their case of settlement of C.S. Plot No.310 with them on the basis of the Kabuliyat, Ext.3(a) was examined by the trial Court as well as by the Court of first appeal who recorded the concurrent finding that those rent receipt were fabricated documents, The learned Judges of the High Court appear to have expressed disagreement with the aforesaid finding on the view that in judging this question the said Court had committed an error in regard to the burden of proof and that, as such, their finding was not tenable in law. We do not think that the learned Judges of the High Court were correct in their view that the findings of the Courts below on the question of the genuineness of the rent receipts had been vitiated by a wrong view of the burden of proof and were justified in rejecting the said finding for the purpose of the disposal of the appeal. 

 19. The finding of the two courts of fact that the plaintiffs were initially inducted upon the disputed land as bargadars under Mainuddin was dependent, to a certain extent, upon their finding on the question of the plaintiff's title, as sought to be established at the trial court by adducing evidence. The plaintiff's case is that the jote of Mani Mohan Dutta, as recorded in Khatian No.82, was auction purchased by the heirs of the decree-holders, Haladar Dey Sarkar, and was thereafter settled with the plaintiffs on 15.1.41 by a Kabuliyat Ext.13(a). The greatest hindrance, found by the Courts below, to the acceptance of the story of settlement as sought to be made out by the plaintiffs, was the character of Mainuddin's interest as recorded in Khatian No.83 of mouza Rajarbagh and the complete absence of any pleading as to how the said interest was extinguished. Both of the said Courts took the view that the entries in the Khatian clearly showed that the interest of Mainuddin was that of an occupancy raiyat which was protected under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act and, therefore, by the auction sale of the superior right of his landlord, who was a tenure holder his interest as a raiyat was not affected at all. It was pointed out by the trial Court that even if it was held that the interest of Mainuddin was an under raiyati, not protected under section 160 of the Act, it would be an encumbrance which required a notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act for its annulment and that the service of any such notice having not been pleaded nor proved, the interest of Mainuddin could not be extinguished. At the time of the trial a new case as to the surrender by Mainuddin of his interest was sought to be established by proving a Kabuliyat Ext.3. In respect of C.S. plot No.311 and by adducing oral evidence to show that possession of plot No.311 was given up by Mainuddin in favour of the auction purchasers. The story of the surrender of the lands of C.S. Khatian No.83 and the giving up of possession of C.S plot No.310 was completely disbelieved by the said two Courts on an analysis of the oral and documentary evidence adduced by the parties in respect thereof and on a consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case. One of the points considered by the said Courts in this connection was that the homestead of Mainuddin was not confined to C.S. plot No.311 only but it spread over to a part of C.S. plot No.310 as well. 

 20. The learned Judges of the High Court appear to have expressed to view that the findings of the Courts below that the interest of Mainuddin was protected under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act having been reached without considering the provision contained in section 48G (3) of the Act which lays down that the right of occupancy enjoyed by an under raiyat should not be a protected interest under section 160 of the Act are not tenable in law. This view of the High Court is based upon the assumption that the interest of Mainuddin was that of an under raiyat, but there appears to be absolutely no basis for such an assumption. On a consideration of the entries of the Khatian No.82 and 83 of Mouza Rajarbagb, Ext. 6 and 6(a) both the Courts below came to the view that Mainuddin was a raiyat having a right of occupancy under Mani Mohan Dutta, who was a tenure holder. As a matter of fact, in the said Khatian the superior landlord of Mainuddin was specifically described as "Madhya Swatwadhlkary chiro-sthayee (i.e. parmanent tenure holder) and Mainuddin was stated to be a 'raiyat Sthitiban' i.e. settled raiyat of the village having regard to the said specific description as to Mainuddin being a settled ratyat having a right of occupancy there is hardly any scope for the court to conceive that Mainuddin was an under raiyat. 

 21. The learned Judges of the High Court seem to have been carried away by the term 'Kole jote’ which was stated to be the interest of Mainuddin in the said khatians, presumably on the assumption that the term 'Jote' invariably indicated the interest of a raiyat. This assumption of the learned Judges is obviously not correct because the term 'Jote' is a general term and sometimes used also to indicate the interest of a tenure holder and it is not necessarily equivalent to a raiyati jote, as was observed by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Midnapore Zamindary Co. Vs. Naresb Narayan Singh L.R. 48 I.A. 49. I.L.R.48 Cal. 460 AIR 1922 P.C. 241. Similarly in the case of Krishna Nath Sarker Vs. Uani Kusam Kumar Das, AIR 1923 Cal.351 it was held by a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court that the expression 'Jote' was a general term and did not necessarily mean a raiyati and in the facts of that case it was held to be a tenure. On the other hand in the case of Upendra Kishore Sarkar Vs. Sk Khalil, AIR. 1937 Cal. 568: 55 C.LJ, 170 it was held by another Division Bench of the said High Court that the word ‘Jote' might mean even an under raiyati. In the case of Sariatullah Vs. Joinuddin A.I.R 1935 Cal, 463; 39 C.W.N.454. Nasim Ali, J. of the Calcutta high Court in holding that the word 'Jote' did indicate in the facts of that case that it was a tenure made the following observation— 

 22. Even if the view that the term 'Jote' must neceesarily mean a raiyati Jote and 'Kol-jote' similarly would mean an under raiyat, both the Courts of fact having accepted the status of Mainuddin to be that of a raiyat on the basis of the specific description of such interest to be a raiyati and the jote of the superior landlord as a tenure, the learned Judges of the High Court were not justified in taking the said interest to be an under raiyati without properly coming to a finding that the description of Mainuddin to be a raiat and of his landlord to be a tenure holder in the Khatian was incorrect. The learned Judges of the High Court were not therefore correct in assuming the status of Mani Mohan Dutta the superior landlord of Mainuddin, as that of a raiyat and that of Mainuddin as an under raiyat simply from the description of their interest as Jote and koljote respectively in the C.S Khatian No.83. The term jote is a general expression and means a tenancy and the status of a holder of such a tenancy i.e. whether it is that of a tenure holder or of a raiyat will depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. So far as the entries in Khatian No. 83 is concerned the specific nature of the tenancy as described in the terms 'Jote’ and 'Kol jot' were clearly spelt out by the use of expressions Chiro sthayee Madhya Swatwadhikary and sthitiban Raiyat in the Khatian itself, which give rise to statutory presumption as to the correctness of such description. No case as to the incorrectness of these entries in the Khatian was pleaded in the plaint nor any rebutting evidence was adduced by the plaintiffs at the time of the trial, although it was contended at the time of argument that the interest of Mainuddin was not that of raiyat and as such was not protected under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The learned Subordinate-Judge pointed out in his judgment that the term 'Jote' was ambiguous and might mean also tenure and also that it had been admitted by P.W.14, a relation and agent of Haladar Dey Sarkar, the superior landlord of Mani Mohan Dutta, that the status of Mani Mohan Dutta was that of a tenure holder. So the learned Subordinate Judge had no difficulty in coming to the finding that the interest of Mainuddin was that of an occupancy raiyat protected under section 160 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. On appeal this view was affirmed by the Court of the Additional District Judge. It is significant, as it appears from the judgment of the said Court that no issue was joined on this question on behalf of the plaintiffs and that it was conceded by the learned lawyer appearing on behalf of the appellants in the said appeal that the status of Mainuddin was that of an occupancy raiyat. In the Second Appeal, however, this question appears to have been raised by the learned lawyer on behalf of the appellants in spite of their concession on this point in the last court of fact and the learned Judges of the High Court appear to have failed to take notice of the concurrent findings of the Courts below on this question and seem to have been carried away by the expression 'Koljote' as mentioned in the Khatian and assumed that such expression necessarily meant an under raiyati. The learned Judges appear to have held on the basis of such assumption that the provisions of section 48(G) 3 of the Act was attracted and as such the interest of Mainuddin was not a protected interest under section 160 of the Act. 

 23. It has been pointed out above that there is absolutely no basis for this assumption We have pointed out that the question whether Mainuddin was a raiyat or an under raiyat at is a question of fact and the entries in the C.S. Khatian raised a presumption in favour of the correctness of the entries made in the said khatian. In the absence of any rebutting evidence both the Courts below came to a concurrent finding as to the status of Mainuddin being that of a raiyat, relying upon the said entries and also upon the evidence and the facts and circumstances of the case. No error of law or procedure affecting the merits of the case were pointed out in regard to the said finding and as such the said finding was binding upon the High Court in the Second Appeal.
